title: Security essentials
summary: Passwords, multi-factor authentication, devices, data handling and reporting incidents.
body_md:
## Why this matters

Most security incidents start with an ordinary mistake: a reused password, a lost laptop, a file shared with the
wrong person. You don't need to be a security expert to prevent them. You need a few habits, done every time.

## Passwords and passphrases

- Use a **long passphrase**: four or more unrelated words is stronger and easier to remember than a short, complex
  password.
- **Never reuse** a work password anywhere else. When another site is breached, attackers try the same password
  on work systems.
- Keep passwords in the **company password manager**, not in notes, spreadsheets or browser exports.
- Nobody from IT, security or management will ever ask for your password. Treat any request as an attack.

## Multi-factor authentication (MFA)

MFA means a stolen password alone isn't enough to sign in. Turn it on wherever it's offered and use an
authenticator app or security key rather than SMS where you can.

If you get an MFA prompt you didn't start, **deny it and report it**. It means someone already has your password.

## Your devices

- Lock your screen whenever you step away (Windows + L, or Control + Command + Q on a Mac).
- Keep your operating system and browser updated; restart when prompted.
- Don't disable disk encryption, antivirus or device management.
- Report a lost or stolen device **immediately**, even outside working hours. Fast reporting lets us wipe it.

## Handling data

- Store work files only in approved company tools.
- Before sharing a link, check who can open it. "Anyone with the link" is public.
- Don't paste customer data, source code or confidential documents into public AI tools or websites that the
  company hasn't approved.
- Use real personal data only where your job needs it. Test systems should use masked or synthetic data.

## Reporting incidents

Report anything suspicious straight away through the security channel: a suspicious email, a misdirected file,
a lost device, an unusual MFA prompt, or a system behaving strangely. Under the CERT-In Directions, many incident
types must be reported to the government within **6 hours** of being noticed, so minutes matter. You will never
be blamed for reporting in good faith.

quiz.q: Which of these is the strongest password choice?
options: Acme@2026
four unrelated words like velvet-orbit-mango-ladder
Your name and date of birth
The same strong password you use for your personal email

quiz.q: You receive an MFA approval prompt on your phone that you didn't start. What should you do?
options: Approve it so it stops appearing
Ignore it
Deny it and report it to security, then change your password
Turn off MFA

quiz.q: Your laptop is stolen on a Saturday evening. When should you report it?
options: Immediately, even though it's the weekend
On Monday morning
Only if it had customer data on it
At the next team meeting

quiz.q: A colleague asks you to share a customer list through a public file-sharing link. What's the right approach?
options: Use "anyone with the link" so it's quick
Email it to their personal address
Share it in an approved company tool with access limited to the people who need it
Paste it into a chat with the whole company

quiz.q: Why does incident reporting need to be fast?
options: It doesn't; incidents can wait for a weekly review
Many incidents must be reported to CERT-In within 6 hours of being noticed
So the person who caused it can be identified
Reports are only needed for data breaches
